Package org.jdesktop.lg3d.mandela.vm

Class VM

java.lang.Object
org.jdesktop.lg3d.mandela.vm.VM
All Implemented Interfaces:
Machine
public final class VM extends Object implements Machine
The Mandela virtual machine: a two-word-per-instruction stack interpreter.

Everything the compiler promises is settled here and nowhere else. One shared operand stack grows as deep as the values need; one chain of Frame records holds the activations; the dispatch loop reads code[ip] and code[ip + 1] and does not call a method to fetch them. There is no IR, no peephole pass and no JIT: the language is a desktop scripting language, and an interpreter that stays this small is fast enough for panels, widgets and page scripts while costing nothing to start up.

Re-entrancy

A built-in has to be able to run script code — map { } calls a callback, a widget's onClick fires a handler long after the script that installed it returned. Java cannot "step into" the interpreter loop from the middle of it, so the loop cooperates: invoke(org.jdesktop.lg3d.mandela.values.Callable, java.lang.Object, java.lang.Object[]) pushes a frame and marks it as the barrier, and the dispatch loop that is already running picks the frame up and stops the moment that frame returns. The return value is then handed straight back to the native caller instead of being pushed onto the stack the outer expression is still building. Nested callbacks therefore cost one Java frame each, and Capabilities.maxDepth() bounds both the script frames and the nesting.

Errors

A Mandela error is a Java exception on the way out of an instruction and a stacked value on the way into a catch. dispatchError(org.jdesktop.lg3d.mandela.values.MandelaError) walks the frame chain for a live handler, runs the defer bodies of every frame it discards, and stops at the barrier: past that point the exception resumes travelling up through the native call that caught it, into the outer loop, which looks for handlers there. This is what lets an error thrown inside a map callback be caught by a try in the calling script.

Thread safety

None, on purpose. A machine runs one script on one thread; a desktop that wants scripts in parallel builds one machine per thread, each with its own globals and its own budget.

    • setOutput

      public void setOutput(VM.Output standardOut, VM.Output standardError)
      Installs the two console channels. Either may be null, in which case writing to it fails the way a missing capability does.

      Both are raw character sinks: the machine decides where a line ends, so a host that shows whole lines (a browser console, an editor panel) and a host that pipes a stream (the CLI) both work without guessing.

      Parameters:
      standardOut - where print and println go
      standardError - where eprintln and uncaught errors go
